al-Mubarrad said: *al-fasila* is a piece of the body's limbs, and a man's clan is called *fasila* by likening it to a part of him.

Malik said: *al-fasila* is the one who raises him.

﴿And whoever is on earth, all of them﴾: meaning the criminal would wish that if he ransomed himself with all who are on earth of the two species (*thaqalan*, i.e., humans and jinn) and others of creation, it would be enough for him.

---

*Note on ʿAdhab and ascending stairways (ma'arij): the Arabic term "ma'arij" is rendered as "ascending stairways," with the Arabic transliteration given in the sense of the plural of "mi'raj" in the commentary's usage.*

Its statement, "Thumma yunjihi" (then it would save him), is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "yaftadi" (would ransom himself): meaning, he would wish to ransom himself, and then the ransom would save him. The conjunction with thumma (then) is used to indicate the improbability of salvation. It has also been said that "yawaddu" (he would wish) requires an answer, as in His statement: ﴿They wish that you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ [al-Qalam: 9], and the answer here would be "thumma yunjihi." The first view is preferable.

His statement, "Kalla" (No!), is a rebuke to the criminal for that desire, and a clarification that what he wished for, namely the ransom, is impossible. "Kalla" comes with the meaning of "haqqan" (truly), and with the meaning of "la" (no), while including the sense of restraint and rebuke. The pronoun in (p-1530) His statement: ﴿Indeed, it is Laza⦗Laẓā⦘﴾ refers to Jahannam. Its derivation is from talazzi (blazing) in the fire, which is blazing. It has also been said that its origin is lazaẓ, meaning the continuation of punishment, so one of the two ẓā's was changed to an alif. It has also been said that Laẓā is the second rank of the levels of Jahannam.

﴿Nazzā‘atan lilshawā⦘﴾: al-Jumhur read "nazzā‘atun" with a raised vowel (ḍammah), taking it as a second predicate of "inna," or the predicate of an omitted subject, or Laẓā may be a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in the accusative case, and "nazzā‘atun" the predicate of "inna." Or "nazzā‘atun" is an adjective (ṣifah) of Laẓā on the assumption that it is not a proper name. Or the pronoun in "annahā" refers to the event/matter (al-qiṣṣah), so Laẓā is the subject and "nazzā‘atun" its predicate, and the whole sentence is the predicate of "inna." Ḥafṣ on the authority of ‘Āṣim, and Abū ‘Amr in one narration from him, and Abū Ḥaywah, al-Za‘farānī, al-Tirmidhī, and Ibn Miqsam read "nazzā‘atan" with a fatḥah, as a circumstantial (ḥāl).

Abū ‘Alī al-Fārisī said: taking it as a circumstantial is remote, because there is nothing in the sentence that governs the circumstantial. It has been said that the governing element is what the sentence implies of the meaning of blazing, or it is an accusative of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ). Al-Shawā means the extremities, or it is the plural of shawāh, which is the skin of the head, and from it is the verse of al-A‘shā:

"Qālat Qatīlatu mā lahu * qad jullilat shaybān shawātuhu"

Al-Ḥasan and Thābit al-Bunānī said: ﴿nazzā‘atan lilshawā⦘, meaning: it strips away the beauty and comeliness of the face. Abū al-‘Āliyah and Qatādah said likewise: it strips the flesh and skin from the bone, leaving nothing in it.

Al-Kisā’ī said: they are the joints.

Abū Ṣāliḥ said: they are the extremities of the two hands and two feet.

﴿Tad‘ū man adbar⦘, i.e., Laẓā calls whoever turned his back on the truth in the world and ﴿tawallā⦘, i.e., turned away from it.

﴿Wa jama‘a fa-awʿā⦘, i.e., he gathered wealth and put it in a container. It has been said: it will say, "Come to me, O polytheist! Come to me, O hypocrite!" It has also been said: the meaning of "tad‘ū" is "tuhlik" (destroys); the Arabs say, "da‘āka Allāh," i.e., "Allah destroy you." It has also been said: it is not calling by tongue, but its calling them is its capability to punish them. It has also been said: the intended meaning is that the guards of Jahannam call the disbelievers and hypocrites, and the calling is attributed to the Fire, by way of attributing what belongs to the inhabitants to the place. It has also been said: it is a figure of speech and imagery, with no actual calling; the meaning is that their final destination is to it, as the poet said:

"Wa laqad habaṭnā al-wād bayna quwādinā * nad‘ū al-anīsa bihi al-ghaṣīṣu al-abkamu"

Al-Ghaṣīṣ al-abkam is the fly, and it does not call. In this there is a censure of one who gathers wealth, stores it, hoards it, and does not spend it in the paths of good, or does not pay its zakāt.

Al-Firyābī, ‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Nasā’ī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ‘Abbās concerning His statement: ﴿A questioner asked⦘, he said: it is al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, who said, "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky."

And concerning His statement: ﴿with a punishment that will befall⦘, he said: it will occur to the disbelievers, and none can repel it from Allah. ﴿The Lord of the ascending stairways⦘, he said: the Lord of the degrees.

‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him concerning His statement: ﴿A questioner asked⦘, he said: "Sāla" is a valley in Jahannam.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him also concerning His statement: ﴿The Lord of the ascending stairways⦘, he said: the Lord of exaltedness and bounties.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him also concerning His statement: ﴿in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years⦘, he said: the extent of His command from the lowest of the earths to the extent of His command from above the seven heavens is the measure of fifty thousand years. And ﴿a Day whose measure is a thousand years⦘ [al-Sajdah: 5], he said: it means the command descends from the sky to the earth and ascends from the earth to the sky in one day, and that is the measure of a thousand years, because the distance between the sky and the earth is a journey of five hundred years.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim also reported from him, saying: the thickness of each earth is five hundred years, the thickness of each heaven is five hundred years, the distance between each earth is five hundred years, and from heaven to heaven is five hundred years; that is His statement: ﴿in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years⦘.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th reported from him also concerning His statement: ﴿in a Day whose measure is a thousand years of what you count⦘, he said: this is in the world, where the angels ascend in a day whose measure is a thousand years of what you count. And concerning His statement: ﴿in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years⦘, this is the Day of Resurrection, which Allah made for the disbeliever to be the measure of fifty thousand years.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Bayhaqī reported from him also concerning His statement: ﴿in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years⦘, he said: If you were to measure it, it would be fifty thousand years of your days.

He said: meaning the Day of Resurrection.

We have already mentioned from Ibn ‘Abbās the pause in combining the two verses in Sūrat al-Sajdah.

Aḥmad, Abū Ya‘lā, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th reported from Abū Sa‘īd al-Khudrī, who said: It was said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years⦘, how long this day is!" He said: "By He in whose hand is my soul, it will be made light for the believer until it is easier for him than an obligatory prayer he prays in the world."

In its chain is Darrāj from Abū al-Haytham, and both are weak.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th reported from Abū Hurayrah, raised (marfū‘): "The length of the Day of Resurrection for the believers is only like the time between Ẓuhr and ‘Aṣr."

al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī in Nawādir al-Uṣūl reported from Ibn ‘Abbās concerning His statement: ﴿So be patient with patience beautiful⦘, he said: do not complain to anyone except Me.

Aḥmad, ‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Khaṭīb in al-Muttafiq wa al-Muftariq, and al-Ḍiyā’ in al-Mukhtārah reported from Ibn ‘Abbās concerning His statement: ﴿On the Day the sky will be like molten brass⦘, he said: like the dregs of oil.

Ibn Jarīr reported from him, he said: ﴿They will be made to see them⦘: some of them will recognize others, and they will know one another, then some of them will flee from others.

Ibn Jarīr also reported from him concerning His statement: ﴿Nazzā‘atan lilshawā⦘, he said: it pulls out the top of the head.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 70, verses 1–18 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan.
Al-Qurtubi said: by consensus.
Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "A surah was revealed in Mecca, [beginning with] *Sa'ala* (one asked)."
Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿A questioner asked about a torment about to befall﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read *sa'ala* with a hamza, while Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir read it without a hamza. Whoever reads it with a hamza takes it from *al-su'al* (asking), and this is the common usage. It may be that it is an implicit meaning of *al-du'a'* (invoking), which is why it takes the *ba'* (with), as you say *da'awtu li-kadha* (I invoked for such-and-such). The meaning is: a caller invoked against himself a torment about to befall. It is also permissible that it retains its original sense, with the *ba'* meaning *ʿan* (about), as in His saying: ﴿ask about Him one who is informed﴾ [al-Furqan: 59]. As for the one who did not read the hamza, it is either a lightening of the hamza by converting it to an *alif*, in which case its meaning is the meaning of the reading of the one who read the hamza, or it is from *al-sayalan* (flowing), and the meaning is: a valley in Hell flowed, called *Sa'il*, as Zayd ibn Thabit said.

This is supported by the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas: *sala sayl* (a flood flowed). It was also said that *sala* means *iltamasa* (sought), and the meaning is: a seeker sought a torment for the disbelievers, so the *ba'* is extra, as in His saying: ﴿grows with oil﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 20]. The first meaning is the apparent one.

al-Akhfash said: it is said, "We went out asking about so-and-so and with so-and-so."

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: when it is from *al-su'al* (asking), its origin is that it transitively takes two objects, and it is permissible to limit it to one of them, and it takes the other by a preposition.

This questioner was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, when he said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful torment﴾. He was among those killed on the Day of Badr by being executed in captivity (sabran). It was also said that he was Abu Jahl, and it was said that he was al-Harith ibn al-Nuʿman al-Fihri.

The first is more likely, for the reason that will come.

Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read *sala sal* (like *mala mal*), with the original being *sa'il*, and the ʿayn was deleted for lightness, as it is said *shak fi shaʾik al-silah* (a rusted weapon).

It was also said: the questioner was Nuh (peace be upon him), who asked for torment upon the disbelievers. It was also said: it was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who invoked punishment upon them. His saying ﴿with a torment about to befall﴾ means either in this world, like the Day of Badr, or in the Hereafter.

His saying *lil-kafirin* (for the disbelievers) is another attribute of *ʿadhab* (torment), meaning: existing for the disbelievers; or it is connected to *waqiʿ* (about to befall), and the *lam* is for cause; or to *sa'ala*, with it implicitly meaning *daʿa* (invoked); or it is in a place of nominative case by an assumption: it is for the disbelievers; or the *lam* means *ʿala* (upon). This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: *bi-ʿadhabin waqiʿin ʿala al-kafirin* (upon the disbelievers).

al-Farra' said: the estimate is: a torment for the disbelievers, befalling them. So *al-waqiʿ* is an attribute of *ʿadhab*. The clause ﴿there is none to avert it﴾ is another attribute of *ʿadhab*, or a circumstantial clause from it, or a resumed (new) sentence. The meaning is: that torment which befalls them cannot be averted by anyone.

His saying ﴿from Allah﴾ is connected to *waqiʿ*, meaning: befalling from His direction, glorified be He; or to *dafiʿ* (averter), meaning: there is no averter from His direction, exalted be He.

﴿Lord of the ascending stairways﴾: meaning the degrees by which the angels ascend. al-Kalbi said: they are the heavens, and He named them *maʿarij* (ascending stairways) because the angels ascend through them. It was also said: the *maʿarij* are the levels of Allah's blessings upon creation; it was also said: the *maʿarij* are the greatness; it was also said: they are the upper chambers.

Ibn Mas'ud read *dhi al-maʿarib* with an added *ya'*. It is said: *maʿarij* and *maʿarib*, like *mafatih* and *mafatib*.

﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him﴾: meaning they rise through those ascending stairways which Allah made for them. The majority read *taʿruju* with the feminine prefix, while Ibn Mas'ud and his companions, al-Kisa'i, and al-Sulami read it with the masculine prefix. "The Spirit" is Jibril, singled out for mention after the angels because of his nobility. This is supported by His saying: ﴿the Trustworthy Spirit brought it down﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 193]. It was also said: "the Spirit" here is another great angel other than Jibril.

Abu Salih said: it is one of the creatures of Allah, glorified be He, in the form of humans, though they are not humans.

Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb said: it is the spirit of the dead person when he is taken.

The first is more likely.

The meaning of *ilayhi* (to Him) is: to the place where they end up. It was also said: to His Throne. It was also said: it is like the saying of Ibrahim: ﴿I am going to my Lord﴾ [al-Saffat: 99], meaning: to where my Lord commanded me, in a day whose measure was fifty thousand years.

Ibn Ishaq, al-Kalbi, and Wahb ibn Munabbih said: that is, the angels ascend to the place which is their abode, in a time whose measure, for others, if they ascended, would be fifty thousand years. Mujahid also said this.

ʿIkrima said, and it is narrated from Mujahid, that the duration of the lifespan of this world is this measure; no one knows how much has passed or how much remains, and none knows that except Allah.

Qatada, al-Kalbi, and Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: the intended meaning is the Day of Resurrection, meaning that the measure of the matter in it, if another than Allah, glorified be He, were to undertake it, would be fifty thousand years, while He, glorified be He, finishes with it in an hour. It was also said: the duration of the standing of the servants for reckoning is this measure, and after that the people of Paradise settle in Paradise, and the people of the Fire in the Fire.

It was also said: the measure of the Day of Resurrection for the disbelievers is fifty thousand years, while for the believers it is the measure of what is between noon and afternoon prayer.

It was also said: this measure is mentioned merely as an illustration and imagery for the extreme height of those ascending stairways and the remoteness of their reach; or for the length of the Day of Resurrection in consideration of the hardships and miseries it contains, just as the Arabs describe days of hardship as long and days of joy as short. They compare a short day to the *ibham* of the *qata'* (a bird's sitting-space, i.e., a very brief span) and a long day to the shadow of a spear. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"And a day like the shadow of a spear, its length shortened by the blood of the wineskin far from us, and the lining up of the lutes."*

It was also said: there is a transposition in the speech, meaning: there is no averter from Allah, Lord of the ascending stairways, on a day whose measure is fifty thousand years, when the angels and the Spirit ascend to Him. We have already mentioned the reconciliation between this verse and His saying in Surat al-Sajda: ﴿on a day whose measure is a thousand years﴾ [al-Sajda: 5], so refer back to it.

It has been said regarding the reconciliation: from the lowest part of the world to the Throne is fifty thousand years, and from the highest heaven of this world to the earth is a thousand years, because the thickness of each heaven is five hundred years, and what is between the lowest part of the heaven and the bottom of the earth is five hundred years. So the meaning is: when the angels ascend from the lowest part of the world to the Throne, the distance of that is fifty thousand years; and if they ascend from this earth in which we are to the inner side of this heaven which is the lowest heaven, the distance of that is a thousand years. What supports this from Ibn ʿAbbas will come at the end of the discussion.

Then Allah, glorified be He, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to be patient, saying: ﴿So be patient with gracious patience﴾. That is: be patient, O Muhammad, over their denial of you and their disbelief in what you have brought, with a gracious patience in which there is no impatience and no complaint to anyone other than Allah. This is the meaning of gracious patience. It was also said: it is that the person afflicted by a calamity is among the people without it being known that he is afflicted. Ibn Zayd and others said: it has been abrogated (naskh, i.e., replaced in ruling) by the verse of the sword.

﴿Indeed, they see it as far off﴾: meaning they see the torment that befalls them as far off, or they see the Day of Resurrection as far off, meaning: not occurring, because they do not believe in it. So the meaning of *baʿidan* (far off) is: deemed remote and impossible. The intended meaning is not that they see it as far but not near.

al-Aʿmash said: they see the resurrection as far off because they do not believe in it, as if they deem it remote by way of impossibility, as you say to one you are debating: "This is far-fetched," meaning: it will not happen.

﴿And We see it as near﴾: meaning We know it to be occurring as near, because what is coming is near.

It was also said: the meaning is: and We see it as easy in Our power, not difficult nor impossible. The sentence is a reason for the command to be patient.

Then Allah, glorified be He, informed when the torment will befall them, saying: ﴿On the day when the sky will be like molten brass﴾. The time expression is connected to an implied element indicated by *waqiʿ* (befalling), or it is a substitute for His saying ﴿on a day﴾, according to the assumption that it is connected to *waqiʿ*; or it is connected to *qarib* (near), or it is determined after it, meaning: on the day when it will be such-and-such. Or it is a substitute for the pronoun in *narahu* (We see it). The first is more likely.

The estimate is: the torment befalls them on the day when the sky will be like *al-muhl*. *Al-muhl* is what is melted of copper, lead, and silver.

Mujahid said: it is pus from the matter and blood.

ʿIkrima and others said: it is the dregs of oil. Its explanation has already been given in Surat al-Kahf and al-Dukhan.

﴿And the mountains will be like wool of various colors﴾: meaning like dyed wool. *ʿIhn* (wool) is not said of wool unless it is dyed.

al-Hasan said: the mountains will be like *ʿihn*, which is red wool, the weakest of wool. It was also said: *ʿihn* is wool of various colors, so He likened the mountains to it in their being of various colors, as in His saying: ﴿white and red streaks of various colors, and jet-black﴾ [Fatir: 27]. When they are carded and scattered into the air, they resemble carded *ʿihn* when the wind scatters it.

﴿And no close friend will ask a close friend﴾: meaning no relative will ask his relative about his condition on that day, because of the terrors that have befallen them, which distract the relative from his relative and the intimate friend from his intimate friend, as He, glorified be He, said: ﴿For every person among them on that day is a matter that occupies him﴾ [ʿAbasa: 37]. It was also said: the meaning is: no close friend asks about a close friend; the preposition was deleted and the verb was connected directly.

The majority read *la yasʾalu* in the active voice. It was said: the second object is omitted, and the estimate is: he does not ask him for his help nor his intercession. Abu Jaʿfar, Abu Haywa, Shayba, and Ibn Kathir in one narration read it in the passive voice. al-Bazzi transmitted this reading from ʿAsim, and the meaning is: no close friend is asked to bring his close friend (into presence). It was also said: this reading is by dropping the preposition, meaning: no close friend is asked about a close friend, rather every person asks about himself and about his deeds.

The clause ﴿they will be made to see them﴾ is either a resumed sentence, or an attribute of *hamim* (close friend), meaning: every close friend is made to see his close friend, and none of them is hidden from another.

There is no creature in the Resurrection but it is before the eyes of its companion. They will not ask one another, nor will any of them speak to another, because each one is occupied with himself. Ibn Zayd said: Allah makes the disbelievers in the Fire see those who misled them in the world, namely the leaders who were followed.

It was also said: His saying "they are made to see them" refers to the angels, meaning: they know the conditions of the people, which are not hidden from them. The pronoun in *yubassaruna-hum* is plural, though the two are the two close friends, in consideration of the general sense, because they are indefinite nouns in a negative context. The majority read *yubassaruna-hum* with the doubled *ba'*, and Qatada read it with the single *ba'*.

Then He, glorified be He, began speech, saying: ﴿The criminal would wish he could ransom himself from the torment of that day with his children﴾. The intended meaning of "criminal" is the disbeliever, or everyone who has committed a sin deserving the Fire. He would wish to ransom himself from the torment of the Day of Resurrection which has befallen him ﴿with his children﴾, ﴿his spouse and his brother﴾, for these are the most beloved people to him and the most honored in his sight. If ransom were accepted from him, he would ransom himself with them and be freed from the torment that has befallen him. The sentence is resumed to explain that the preoccupation of each criminal with himself reaches a point where he wishes to ransom himself from the torment with those mentioned.

The majority read ﴿from the torment of that day﴾ with *ʿadhab* construed as genitive of *yawmi'idhin* (that day). Abu Haywa read *ʿadhabin* with tanwin and cut the genitive construction. The majority read *yawma'idhin* with a kasra on the *mim*, while Nafi', al-Kisa'i, al-Aʿraj, and Abu Haywa read it with a fatha on it.

﴿And his kin who shelters him﴾: meaning his nearest relatives who unite him in lineage or who take him in during hardships, and to whom he takes refuge.

Abu ʿUbayd said: *al-fasila* is less than the *qabila* (tribe).

Tha'lab said: they are his nearest fathers.

al-Mubarrad said: *al-fasila* is a piece of the body's limbs, and a man's clan is called *fasila* by likening it to a part of him.

Malik said: *al-fasila* is the one who raises him.

﴿And whoever is on earth, all of them﴾: meaning the criminal would wish that if he ransomed himself with all who are on earth of the two species (*thaqalan*, i.e., humans and jinn) and others of creation, it would be enough for him.

---

The conjunction with thumma (then) is used to indicate the improbability of salvation. It has also been said that "yawaddu" (he would wish) requires an answer, as in His statement: ﴿They wish that you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ [al-Qalam: 9], and the answer here would be "thumma yunjihi." The first view is preferable.

His statement, "Kalla" (No!), is a rebuke to the criminal for that desire, and a clarification that what he wished for, namely the ransom, is impossible. "Kalla" comes with the meaning of "haqqan" (truly), and with the meaning of "la" (no), while including the sense of restraint and rebuke. The pronoun in (p-1530) His statement: ﴿Indeed, it is Laza⦗Laẓā⦘﴾ refers to Jahannam. Its derivation is from talazzi (blazing) in the fire, which is blazing. It has also been said that its origin is lazaẓ, meaning the continuation of punishment, so one of the two ẓā's was changed to an alif. It has also been said that Laẓā is the second rank of the levels of Jahannam.

﴿Nazzā‘atan lilshawā⦘﴾: al-Jumhur read "nazzā‘atun" with a raised vowel (ḍammah), taking it as a second predicate of "inna," or the predicate of an omitted subject, or Laẓā may be a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in the accusative case, and "nazzā‘atun" the predicate of "inna." Or "nazzā‘atun" is an adjective (ṣifah) of Laẓā on the assumption that it is not a proper name. Or the pronoun in "annahā" refers to the event/matter (al-qiṣṣah), so Laẓā is the subject and "nazzā‘atun" its predicate, and the whole sentence is the predicate of "inna." Ḥafṣ on the authority of ‘Āṣim, and Abū ‘Amr in one narration from him, and Abū Ḥaywah, al-Za‘farānī, al-Tirmidhī, and Ibn Miqsam read "nazzā‘atan" with a fatḥah, as a circumstantial (ḥāl).

Abū ‘Alī al-Fārisī said: taking it as a circumstantial is remote, because there is nothing in the sentence that governs the circumstantial. It has been said that the governing element is what the sentence implies of the meaning of blazing, or it is an accusative of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ). Al-Shawā means the extremities, or it is the plural of shawāh, which is the skin of the head, and from it is the verse of al-A‘shā:

"Qālat Qatīlatu mā lahu * qad jullilat shaybān shawātuhu"

Al-Ḥasan and Thābit al-Bunānī said: ﴿nazzā‘atan lilshawā⦘, meaning: it strips away the beauty and comeliness of the face. Abū al-‘Āliyah and Qatādah said likewise: it strips the flesh and skin from the bone, leaving nothing in it.

Al-Kisā’ī said: they are the joints.

Abū Ṣāliḥ said: they are the extremities of the two hands and two feet.

﴿Tad‘ū man adbar⦘, i.e., Laẓā calls whoever turned his back on the truth in the world and ﴿tawallā⦘, i.e., turned away from it.

﴿Wa jama‘a fa-awʿā⦘, i.e., he gathered wealth and put it in a container. It has been said: it will say, "Come to me, O polytheist! Come to me, O hypocrite!" It has also been said: the meaning of "tad‘ū" is "tuhlik" (destroys); the Arabs say, "da‘āka Allāh," i.e., "Allah destroy you." It has also been said: it is not calling by tongue, but its calling them is its capability to punish them. It has also been said: the intended meaning is that the guards of Jahannam call the disbelievers and hypocrites, and the calling is attributed to the Fire, by way of attributing what belongs to the inhabitants to the place. It has also been said: it is a figure of speech and imagery, with no actual calling; the meaning is that their final destination is to it, as the poet said:

"Wa laqad habaṭnā al-wād bayna quwādinā * nad‘ū al-anīsa bihi al-ghaṣīṣu al-abkamu"

Al-Ghaṣīṣ al-abkam is the fly, and it does not call. In this there is a censure of one who gathers wealth, stores it, hoards it, and does not spend it in the paths of good, or does not pay its zakāt.

Al-Firyābī, ‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Nasā’ī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ‘Abbās concerning His statement: ﴿A questioner asked⦘, he said: it is al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, who said, "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky."

And concerning His statement: ﴿with a punishment that will befall⦘, he said: it will occur to the disbelievers, and none can repel it from Allah. ﴿The Lord of the ascending stairways⦘, he said: the Lord of the degrees.

‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him concerning His statement: ﴿A questioner asked⦘, he said: "Sāla" is a valley in Jahannam.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him also concerning His statement: ﴿The Lord of the ascending stairways⦘, he said: the Lord of exaltedness and bounties.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him also concerning His statement: ﴿in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years⦘, he said: the extent of His command from the lowest of the earths to the extent of His command from above the seven heavens is the measure of fifty thousand years. And ﴿a Day whose measure is a thousand years⦘ [al-Sajdah: 5], he said: it means the command descends from the sky to the earth and ascends from the earth to the sky in one day, and that is the measure of a thousand years, because the distance between the sky and the earth is a journey of five hundred years.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim also reported from him, saying: the thickness of each earth is five hundred years, the thickness of each heaven is five hundred years, the distance between each earth is five hundred years, and from heaven to heaven is five hundred years; that is His statement: ﴿in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years⦘.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th reported from him also concerning His statement: ﴿in a Day whose measure is a thousand years of what you count⦘, he said: this is in the world, where the angels ascend in a day whose measure is a thousand years of what you count. And concerning His statement: ﴿in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years⦘, this is the Day of Resurrection, which Allah made for the disbeliever to be the measure of fifty thousand years.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Bayhaqī reported from him also concerning His statement: ﴿in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years⦘, he said: If you were to measure it, it would be fifty thousand years of your days.

He said: meaning the Day of Resurrection.

We have already mentioned from Ibn ‘Abbās the pause in combining the two verses in Sūrat al-Sajdah.

Aḥmad, Abū Ya‘lā, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th reported from Abū Sa‘īd al-Khudrī, who said: It was said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years⦘, how long this day is!" He said: "By He in whose hand is my soul, it will be made light for the believer until it is easier for him than an obligatory prayer he prays in the world."

In its chain is Darrāj from Abū al-Haytham, and both are weak.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th reported from Abū Hurayrah, raised (marfū‘): "The length of the Day of Resurrection for the believers is only like the time between Ẓuhr and ‘Aṣr."

al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī in Nawādir al-Uṣūl reported from Ibn ‘Abbās concerning His statement: ﴿So be patient with patience beautiful⦘, he said: do not complain to anyone except Me.

Aḥmad, ‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Khaṭīb in al-Muttafiq wa al-Muftariq, and al-Ḍiyā’ in al-Mukhtārah reported from Ibn ‘Abbās concerning His statement: ﴿On the Day the sky will be like molten brass⦘, he said: like the dregs of oil.

Ibn Jarīr reported from him, he said: ﴿They will be made to see them⦘: some of them will recognize others, and they will know one another, then some of them will flee from others.

Ibn Jarīr also reported from him concerning His statement: ﴿Nazzā‘atan lilshawā⦘, he said: it pulls out the top of the head.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 70, verses 1–18 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan.
Al-Qurtubi said: by consensus.
Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "A surah was revealed in Mecca, [beginning with] *Sa'ala* (one asked)."
Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿A questioner asked about a torment about to befall﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read *sa'ala* with a hamza, while Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir read it without a hamza. Whoever reads it with a hamza takes it from *al-su'al* (asking), and this is the common usage. It may be that it is an implicit meaning of *al-du'a'* (invoking), which is why it takes the *ba'* (with), as you say *da'awtu li-kadha* (I invoked for such-and-such). The meaning is: a caller invoked against himself a torment about to befall. It is also permissible that it retains its original sense, with the *ba'* meaning *ʿan* (about), as in His saying: ﴿ask about Him one who is informed﴾ [al-Furqan: 59]. As for the one who did not read the hamza, it is either a lightening of the hamza by converting it to an *alif*, in which case its meaning is the meaning of the reading of the one who read the hamza, or it is from *al-sayalan* (flowing), and the meaning is: a valley in Hell flowed, called *Sa'il*, as Zayd ibn Thabit said.

This is supported by the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas: *sala sayl* (a flood flowed). It was also said that *sala* means *iltamasa* (sought), and the meaning is: a seeker sought a torment for the disbelievers, so the *ba'* is extra, as in His saying: ﴿grows with oil﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 20]. The first meaning is the apparent one.

al-Akhfash said: it is said, "We went out asking about so-and-so and with so-and-so."

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: when it is from *al-su'al* (asking), its origin is that it transitively takes two objects, and it is permissible to limit it to one of them, and it takes the other by a preposition.

This questioner was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, when he said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful torment﴾. He was among those killed on the Day of Badr by being executed in captivity (sabran). It was also said that he was Abu Jahl, and it was said that he was al-Harith ibn al-Nuʿman al-Fihri.

The first is more likely, for the reason that will come.

Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read *sala sal* (like *mala mal*), with the original being *sa'il*, and the ʿayn was deleted for lightness, as it is said *shak fi shaʾik al-silah* (a rusted weapon).

It was also said: the questioner was Nuh (peace be upon him), who asked for torment upon the disbelievers. It was also said: it was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who invoked punishment upon them. His saying ﴿with a torment about to befall﴾ means either in this world, like the Day of Badr, or in the Hereafter.

His saying *lil-kafirin* (for the disbelievers) is another attribute of *ʿadhab* (torment), meaning: existing for the disbelievers; or it is connected to *waqiʿ* (about to befall), and the *lam* is for cause; or to *sa'ala*, with it implicitly meaning *daʿa* (invoked); or it is in a place of nominative case by an assumption: it is for the disbelievers; or the *lam* means *ʿala* (upon). This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: *bi-ʿadhabin waqiʿin ʿala al-kafirin* (upon the disbelievers).

al-Farra' said: the estimate is: a torment for the disbelievers, befalling them. So *al-waqiʿ* is an attribute of *ʿadhab*. The clause ﴿there is none to avert it﴾ is another attribute of *ʿadhab*, or a circumstantial clause from it, or a resumed (new) sentence. The meaning is: that torment which befalls them cannot be averted by anyone.

His saying ﴿from Allah﴾ is connected to *waqiʿ*, meaning: befalling from His direction, glorified be He; or to *dafiʿ* (averter), meaning: there is no averter from His direction, exalted be He.

﴿Lord of the ascending stairways﴾: meaning the degrees by which the angels ascend. al-Kalbi said: they are the heavens, and He named them *maʿarij* (ascending stairways) because the angels ascend through them. It was also said: the *maʿarij* are the levels of Allah's blessings upon creation; it was also said: the *maʿarij* are the greatness; it was also said: they are the upper chambers.

Ibn Mas'ud read *dhi al-maʿarib* with an added *ya'*. It is said: *maʿarij* and *maʿarib*, like *mafatih* and *mafatib*.

﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him﴾: meaning they rise through those ascending stairways which Allah made for them. The majority read *taʿruju* with the feminine prefix, while Ibn Mas'ud and his companions, al-Kisa'i, and al-Sulami read it with the masculine prefix. "The Spirit" is Jibril, singled out for mention after the angels because of his nobility. This is supported by His saying: ﴿the Trustworthy Spirit brought it down﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 193]. It was also said: "the Spirit" here is another great angel other than Jibril.

Abu Salih said: it is one of the creatures of Allah, glorified be He, in the form of humans, though they are not humans.

Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb said: it is the spirit of the dead person when he is taken.

The first is more likely.

The meaning of *ilayhi* (to Him) is: to the place where they end up. It was also said: to His Throne. It was also said: it is like the saying of Ibrahim: ﴿I am going to my Lord﴾ [al-Saffat: 99], meaning: to where my Lord commanded me, in a day whose measure was fifty thousand years.

Ibn Ishaq, al-Kalbi, and Wahb ibn Munabbih said: that is, the angels ascend to the place which is their abode, in a time whose measure, for others, if they ascended, would be fifty thousand years. Mujahid also said this.

ʿIkrima said, and it is narrated from Mujahid, that the duration of the lifespan of this world is this measure; no one knows how much has passed or how much remains, and none knows that except Allah.

Qatada, al-Kalbi, and Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: the intended meaning is the Day of Resurrection, meaning that the measure of the matter in it, if another than Allah, glorified be He, were to undertake it, would be fifty thousand years, while He, glorified be He, finishes with it in an hour. It was also said: the duration of the standing of the servants for reckoning is this measure, and after that the people of Paradise settle in Paradise, and the people of the Fire in the Fire.

It was also said: the measure of the Day of Resurrection for the disbelievers is fifty thousand years, while for the believers it is the measure of what is between noon and afternoon prayer.

It was also said: this measure is mentioned merely as an illustration and imagery for the extreme height of those ascending stairways and the remoteness of their reach; or for the length of the Day of Resurrection in consideration of the hardships and miseries it contains, just as the Arabs describe days of hardship as long and days of joy as short. They compare a short day to the *ibham* of the *qata'* (a bird's sitting-space, i.e., a very brief span) and a long day to the shadow of a spear. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"And a day like the shadow of a spear, its length shortened by the blood of the wineskin far from us, and the lining up of the lutes."*

It was also said: there is a transposition in the speech, meaning: there is no averter from Allah, Lord of the ascending stairways, on a day whose measure is fifty thousand years, when the angels and the Spirit ascend to Him. We have already mentioned the reconciliation between this verse and His saying in Surat al-Sajda: ﴿on a day whose measure is a thousand years﴾ [al-Sajda: 5], so refer back to it.

It has been said regarding the reconciliation: from the lowest part of the world to the Throne is fifty thousand years, and from the highest heaven of this world to the earth is a thousand years, because the thickness of each heaven is five hundred years, and what is between the lowest part of the heaven and the bottom of the earth is five hundred years. So the meaning is: when the angels ascend from the lowest part of the world to the Throne, the distance of that is fifty thousand years; and if they ascend from this earth in which we are to the inner side of this heaven which is the lowest heaven, the distance of that is a thousand years. What supports this from Ibn ʿAbbas will come at the end of the discussion.

Then Allah, glorified be He, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to be patient, saying: ﴿So be patient with gracious patience﴾. That is: be patient, O Muhammad, over their denial of you and their disbelief in what you have brought, with a gracious patience in which there is no impatience and no complaint to anyone other than Allah. This is the meaning of gracious patience. It was also said: it is that the person afflicted by a calamity is among the people without it being known that he is afflicted. Ibn Zayd and others said: it has been abrogated (naskh, i.e., replaced in ruling) by the verse of the sword.

﴿Indeed, they see it as far off﴾: meaning they see the torment that befalls them as far off, or they see the Day of Resurrection as far off, meaning: not occurring, because they do not believe in it. So the meaning of *baʿidan* (far off) is: deemed remote and impossible. The intended meaning is not that they see it as far but not near.

al-Aʿmash said: they see the resurrection as far off because they do not believe in it, as if they deem it remote by way of impossibility, as you say to one you are debating: "This is far-fetched," meaning: it will not happen.

﴿And We see it as near﴾: meaning We know it to be occurring as near, because what is coming is near.

It was also said: the meaning is: and We see it as easy in Our power, not difficult nor impossible. The sentence is a reason for the command to be patient.

Then Allah, glorified be He, informed when the torment will befall them, saying: ﴿On the day when the sky will be like molten brass﴾. The time expression is connected to an implied element indicated by *waqiʿ* (befalling), or it is a substitute for His saying ﴿on a day﴾, according to the assumption that it is connected to *waqiʿ*; or it is connected to *qarib* (near), or it is determined after it, meaning: on the day when it will be such-and-such. Or it is a substitute for the pronoun in *narahu* (We see it). The first is more likely.

The estimate is: the torment befalls them on the day when the sky will be like *al-muhl*. *Al-muhl* is what is melted of copper, lead, and silver.

Mujahid said: it is pus from the matter and blood.

ʿIkrima and others said: it is the dregs of oil. Its explanation has already been given in Surat al-Kahf and al-Dukhan.

﴿And the mountains will be like wool of various colors﴾: meaning like dyed wool. *ʿIhn* (wool) is not said of wool unless it is dyed.

al-Hasan said: the mountains will be like *ʿihn*, which is red wool, the weakest of wool. It was also said: *ʿihn* is wool of various colors, so He likened the mountains to it in their being of various colors, as in His saying: ﴿white and red streaks of various colors, and jet-black﴾ [Fatir: 27]. When they are carded and scattered into the air, they resemble carded *ʿihn* when the wind scatters it.

﴿And no close friend will ask a close friend﴾: meaning no relative will ask his relative about his condition on that day, because of the terrors that have befallen them, which distract the relative from his relative and the intimate friend from his intimate friend, as He, glorified be He, said: ﴿For every person among them on that day is a matter that occupies him﴾ [ʿAbasa: 37]. It was also said: the meaning is: no close friend asks about a close friend; the preposition was deleted and the verb was connected directly.

The majority read *la yasʾalu* in the active voice. It was said: the second object is omitted, and the estimate is: he does not ask him for his help nor his intercession. Abu Jaʿfar, Abu Haywa, Shayba, and Ibn Kathir in one narration read it in the passive voice. al-Bazzi transmitted this reading from ʿAsim, and the meaning is: no close friend is asked to bring his close friend (into presence). It was also said: this reading is by dropping the preposition, meaning: no close friend is asked about a close friend, rather every person asks about himself and about his deeds.

The clause ﴿they will be made to see them﴾ is either a resumed sentence, or an attribute of *hamim* (close friend), meaning: every close friend is made to see his close friend, and none of them is hidden from another.

There is no creature in the Resurrection but it is before the eyes of its companion. They will not ask one another, nor will any of them speak to another, because each one is occupied with himself. Ibn Zayd said: Allah makes the disbelievers in the Fire see those who misled them in the world, namely the leaders who were followed.

It was also said: His saying "they are made to see them" refers to the angels, meaning: they know the conditions of the people, which are not hidden from them. The pronoun in *yubassaruna-hum* is plural, though the two are the two close friends, in consideration of the general sense, because they are indefinite nouns in a negative context. The majority read *yubassaruna-hum* with the doubled *ba'*, and Qatada read it with the single *ba'*.

Then He, glorified be He, began speech, saying: ﴿The criminal would wish he could ransom himself from the torment of that day with his children﴾. The intended meaning of "criminal" is the disbeliever, or everyone who has committed a sin deserving the Fire. He would wish to ransom himself from the torment of the Day of Resurrection which has befallen him ﴿with his children﴾, ﴿his spouse and his brother﴾, for these are the most beloved people to him and the most honored in his sight. If ransom were accepted from him, he would ransom himself with them and be freed from the torment that has befallen him. The sentence is resumed to explain that the preoccupation of each criminal with himself reaches a point where he wishes to ransom himself from the torment with those mentioned.

The majority read ﴿from the torment of that day﴾ with *ʿadhab* construed as genitive of *yawmi'idhin* (that day). Abu Haywa read *ʿadhabin* with tanwin and cut the genitive construction. The majority read *yawma'idhin* with a kasra on the *mim*, while Nafi', al-Kisa'i, al-Aʿraj, and Abu Haywa read it with a fatha on it.

﴿And his kin who shelters him﴾: meaning his nearest relatives who unite him in lineage or who take him in during hardships, and to whom he takes refuge.

Abu ʿUbayd said: *al-fasila* is less than the *qabila* (tribe).

Tha'lab said: they are his nearest fathers.

al-Mubarrad said: *al-fasila* is a piece of the body's limbs, and a man's clan is called *fasila* by likening it to a part of him.

Malik said: *al-fasila* is the one who raises him.

﴿And whoever is on earth, all of them﴾: meaning the criminal would wish that if he ransomed himself with all who are on earth of the two species (*thaqalan*, i.e., humans and jinn) and others of creation, it would be enough for him.

*Note on ʿAdhab and ascending stairways (ma'arij): the Arabic term "ma'arij" is rendered as "ascending stairways," with the Arabic transliteration given in the sense of the plural of "mi'raj" in the commentary's usage.*

Its statement, "Thumma yunjihi" (then it would save him), is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "yaftadi" (would ransom himself): meaning, he would wish to ransom himself, and then the ransom would save him. The conjunction with thumma (then) is used to indicate the improbability of salvation. It has also been said that "yawaddu" (he would wish) requires an answer, as in His statement: ﴿They wish that you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ [al-Qalam: 9], and the answer here would be "thumma yunjihi." The first view is preferable.

His statement, "Kalla" (No!), is a rebuke to the criminal for that desire, and a clarification that what he wished for, namely the ransom, is impossible. "Kalla" comes with the meaning of "haqqan" (truly), and with the meaning of "la" (no), while including the sense of restraint and rebuke. The pronoun in (p-1530) His statement: ﴿Indeed, it is Laza⦗Laẓā⦘﴾ refers to Jahannam. Its derivation is from talazzi (blazing) in the fire, which is blazing. It has also been said that its origin is lazaẓ, meaning the continuation of punishment, so one of the two ẓā's was changed to an alif. It has also been said that Laẓā is the second rank of the levels of Jahannam.

﴿Nazzā‘atan lilshawā⦘﴾: al-Jumhur read "nazzā‘atun" with a raised vowel (ḍammah), taking it as a second predicate of "inna," or the predicate of an omitted subject, or Laẓā may be a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in the accusative case, and "nazzā‘atun" the predicate of "inna." Or "nazzā‘atun" is an adjective (ṣifah) of Laẓā on the assumption that it is not a proper name. Or the pronoun in "annahā" refers to the event/matter (al-qiṣṣah), so Laẓā is the subject and "nazzā‘atun" its predicate, and the whole sentence is the predicate of "inna." Ḥafṣ on the authority of ‘Āṣim, and Abū ‘Amr in one narration from him, and Abū Ḥaywah, al-Za‘farānī, al-Tirmidhī, and Ibn Miqsam read "nazzā‘atan" with a fatḥah, as a circumstantial (ḥāl).

Abū ‘Alī al-Fārisī said: taking it as a circumstantial is remote, because there is nothing in the sentence that governs the circumstantial. It has been said that the governing element is what the sentence implies of the meaning of blazing, or it is an accusative of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ). Al-Shawā means the extremities, or it is the plural of shawāh, which is the skin of the head, and from it is the verse of al-A‘shā:

"Qālat Qatīlatu mā lahu * qad jullilat shaybān shawātuhu"

Al-Ḥasan and Thābit al-Bunānī said: ﴿nazzā‘atan lilshawā⦘, meaning: it strips away the beauty and comeliness of the face. Abū al-‘Āliyah and Qatādah said likewise: it strips the flesh and skin from the bone, leaving nothing in it.

Al-Kisā’ī said: they are the joints.

Abū Ṣāliḥ said: they are the extremities of the two hands and two feet.

﴿Tad‘ū man adbar⦘, i.e., Laẓā calls whoever turned his back on the truth in the world and ﴿tawallā⦘, i.e., turned away from it.

﴿Wa jama‘a fa-awʿā⦘, i.e., he gathered wealth and put it in a container. It has been said: it will say, "Come to me, O polytheist! Come to me, O hypocrite!" It has also been said: the meaning of "tad‘ū" is "tuhlik" (destroys); the Arabs say, "da‘āka Allāh," i.e., "Allah destroy you." It has also been said: it is not calling by tongue, but its calling them is its capability to punish them. It has also been said: the intended meaning is that the guards of Jahannam call the disbelievers and hypocrites, and the calling is attributed to the Fire, by way of attributing what belongs to the inhabitants to the place. It has also been said: it is a figure of speech and imagery, with no actual calling; the meaning is that their final destination is to it, as the poet said:

"Wa laqad habaṭnā al-wād bayna quwādinā * nad‘ū al-anīsa bihi al-ghaṣīṣu al-abkamu"

Al-Ghaṣīṣ al-abkam is the fly, and it does not call. In this there is a censure of one who gathers wealth, stores it, hoards it, and does not spend it in the paths of good, or does not pay its zakāt.

Al-Firyābī, ‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Nasā’ī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ‘Abbās concerning His statement: ﴿A questioner asked⦘, he said: it is al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, who said, "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky."

And concerning His statement: ﴿with a punishment that will befall⦘, he said: it will occur to the disbelievers, and none can repel it from Allah. ﴿The Lord of the ascending stairways⦘, he said: the Lord of the degrees.

‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him concerning His statement: ﴿A questioner asked⦘, he said: "Sāla" is a valley in Jahannam.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him also concerning His statement: ﴿The Lord of the ascending stairways⦘, he said: the Lord of exaltedness and bounties.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him also concerning His statement: ﴿in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years⦘, he said: the extent of His command from the lowest of the earths to the extent of His command from above the seven heavens is the measure of fifty thousand years. And ﴿a Day whose measure is a thousand years⦘ [al-Sajdah: 5], he said: it means the command descends from the sky to the earth and ascends from the earth to the sky in one day, and that is the measure of a thousand years, because the distance between the sky and the earth is a journey of five hundred years.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim also reported from him, saying: the thickness of each earth is five hundred years, the thickness of each heaven is five hundred years, the distance between each earth is five hundred years, and from heaven to heaven is five hundred years; that is His statement: ﴿in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years⦘.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th reported from him also concerning His statement: ﴿in a Day whose measure is a thousand years of what you count⦘, he said: this is in the world, where the angels ascend in a day whose measure is a thousand years of what you count. And concerning His statement: ﴿in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years⦘, this is the Day of Resurrection, which Allah made for the disbeliever to be the measure of fifty thousand years.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Bayhaqī reported from him also concerning His statement: ﴿in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years⦘, he said: If you were to measure it, it would be fifty thousand years of your days.

He said: meaning the Day of Resurrection.

We have already mentioned from Ibn ‘Abbās the pause in combining the two verses in Sūrat al-Sajdah.

Aḥmad, Abū Ya‘lā, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th reported from Abū Sa‘īd al-Khudrī, who said: It was said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years⦘, how long this day is!" He said: "By He in whose hand is my soul, it will be made light for the believer until it is easier for him than an obligatory prayer he prays in the world."

In its chain is Darrāj from Abū al-Haytham, and both are weak.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th reported from Abū Hurayrah, raised (marfū‘): "The length of the Day of Resurrection for the believers is only like the time between Ẓuhr and ‘Aṣr."

al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī in Nawādir al-Uṣūl reported from Ibn ‘Abbās concerning His statement: ﴿So be patient with patience beautiful⦘, he said: do not complain to anyone except Me.

Aḥmad, ‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Khaṭīb in al-Muttafiq wa al-Muftariq, and al-Ḍiyā’ in al-Mukhtārah reported from Ibn ‘Abbās concerning His statement: ﴿On the Day the sky will be like molten brass⦘, he said: like the dregs of oil.

Ibn Jarīr reported from him, he said: ﴿They will be made to see them⦘: some of them will recognize others, and they will know one another, then some of them will flee from others.

Ibn Jarīr also reported from him concerning His statement: ﴿Nazzā‘atan lilshawā⦘, he said: it pulls out the top of the head.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 70, verses 1–18 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan.
Al-Qurtubi said: by consensus.
Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "A surah was revealed in Mecca, [beginning with] *Sa'ala* (one asked)."
Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿A questioner asked about a torment about to befall﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read *sa'ala* with a hamza, while Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir read it without a hamza. Whoever reads it with a hamza takes it from *al-su'al* (asking), and this is the common usage. It may be that it is an implicit meaning of *al-du'a'* (invoking), which is why it takes the *ba'* (with), as you say *da'awtu li-kadha* (I invoked for such-and-such). The meaning is: a caller invoked against himself a torment about to befall. It is also permissible that it retains its original sense, with the *ba'* meaning *ʿan* (about), as in His saying: ﴿ask about Him one who is informed﴾ [al-Furqan: 59]. As for the one who did not read the hamza, it is either a lightening of the hamza by converting it to an *alif*, in which case its meaning is the meaning of the reading of the one who read the hamza, or it is from *al-sayalan* (flowing), and the meaning is: a valley in Hell flowed, called *Sa'il*, as Zayd ibn Thabit said.

This is supported by the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas: *sala sayl* (a flood flowed). It was also said that *sala* means *iltamasa* (sought), and the meaning is: a seeker sought a torment for the disbelievers, so the *ba'* is extra, as in His saying: ﴿grows with oil﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 20]. The first meaning is the apparent one.

al-Akhfash said: it is said, "We went out asking about so-and-so and with so-and-so."

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: when it is from *al-su'al* (asking), its origin is that it transitively takes two objects, and it is permissible to limit it to one of them, and it takes the other by a preposition.

This questioner was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, when he said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful torment﴾. He was among those killed on the Day of Badr by being executed in captivity (sabran). It was also said that he was Abu Jahl, and it was said that he was al-Harith ibn al-Nuʿman al-Fihri.

The first is more likely, for the reason that will come.

Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud read *sala sal* (like *mala mal*), with the original being *sa'il*, and the ʿayn was deleted for lightness, as it is said *shak fi shaʾik al-silah* (a rusted weapon).

It was also said: the questioner was Nuh (peace be upon him), who asked for torment upon the disbelievers. It was also said: it was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who invoked punishment upon them. His saying ﴿with a torment about to befall﴾ means either in this world, like the Day of Badr, or in the Hereafter.

His saying *lil-kafirin* (for the disbelievers) is another attribute of *ʿadhab* (torment), meaning: existing for the disbelievers; or it is connected to *waqiʿ* (about to befall), and the *lam* is for cause; or to *sa'ala*, with it implicitly meaning *daʿa* (invoked); or it is in a place of nominative case by an assumption: it is for the disbelievers; or the *lam* means *ʿala* (upon). This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: *bi-ʿadhabin waqiʿin ʿala al-kafirin* (upon the disbelievers).

al-Farra' said: the estimate is: a torment for the disbelievers, befalling them. So *al-waqiʿ* is an attribute of *ʿadhab*. The clause ﴿there is none to avert it﴾ is another attribute of *ʿadhab*, or a circumstantial clause from it, or a resumed (new) sentence. The meaning is: that torment which befalls them cannot be averted by anyone.

His saying ﴿from Allah﴾ is connected to *waqiʿ*, meaning: befalling from His direction, glorified be He; or to *dafiʿ* (averter), meaning: there is no averter from His direction, exalted be He.

﴿Lord of the ascending stairways﴾: meaning the degrees by which the angels ascend. al-Kalbi said: they are the heavens, and He named them *maʿarij* (ascending stairways) because the angels ascend through them. It was also said: the *maʿarij* are the levels of Allah's blessings upon creation; it was also said: the *maʿarij* are the greatness; it was also said: they are the upper chambers.

Ibn Mas'ud read *dhi al-maʿarib* with an added *ya'*. It is said: *maʿarij* and *maʿarib*, like *mafatih* and *mafatib*.

﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him﴾: meaning they rise through those ascending stairways which Allah made for them. The majority read *taʿruju* with the feminine prefix, while Ibn Mas'ud and his companions, al-Kisa'i, and al-Sulami read it with the masculine prefix. "The Spirit" is Jibril, singled out for mention after the angels because of his nobility. This is supported by His saying: ﴿the Trustworthy Spirit brought it down﴾ [al-Shuʿara': 193]. It was also said: "the Spirit" here is another great angel other than Jibril.

Abu Salih said: it is one of the creatures of Allah, glorified be He, in the form of humans, though they are not humans.

Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb said: it is the spirit of the dead person when he is taken.

The first is more likely.

The meaning of *ilayhi* (to Him) is: to the place where they end up. It was also said: to His Throne. It was also said: it is like the saying of Ibrahim: ﴿I am going to my Lord﴾ [al-Saffat: 99], meaning: to where my Lord commanded me, in a day whose measure was fifty thousand years.

Ibn Ishaq, al-Kalbi, and Wahb ibn Munabbih said: that is, the angels ascend to the place which is their abode, in a time whose measure, for others, if they ascended, would be fifty thousand years. Mujahid also said this.

ʿIkrima said, and it is narrated from Mujahid, that the duration of the lifespan of this world is this measure; no one knows how much has passed or how much remains, and none knows that except Allah.

Qatada, al-Kalbi, and Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: the intended meaning is the Day of Resurrection, meaning that the measure of the matter in it, if another than Allah, glorified be He, were to undertake it, would be fifty thousand years, while He, glorified be He, finishes with it in an hour. It was also said: the duration of the standing of the servants for reckoning is this measure, and after that the people of Paradise settle in Paradise, and the people of the Fire in the Fire.

It was also said: the measure of the Day of Resurrection for the disbelievers is fifty thousand years, while for the believers it is the measure of what is between noon and afternoon prayer.

It was also said: this measure is mentioned merely as an illustration and imagery for the extreme height of those ascending stairways and the remoteness of their reach; or for the length of the Day of Resurrection in consideration of the hardships and miseries it contains, just as the Arabs describe days of hardship as long and days of joy as short. They compare a short day to the *ibham* of the *qata'* (a bird's sitting-space, i.e., a very brief span) and a long day to the shadow of a spear. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"And a day like the shadow of a spear, its length shortened by the blood of the wineskin far from us, and the lining up of the lutes."*

It was also said: there is a transposition in the speech, meaning: there is no averter from Allah, Lord of the ascending stairways, on a day whose measure is fifty thousand years, when the angels and the Spirit ascend to Him. We have already mentioned the reconciliation between this verse and His saying in Surat al-Sajda: ﴿on a day whose measure is a thousand years﴾ [al-Sajda: 5], so refer back to it.

It has been said regarding the reconciliation: from the lowest part of the world to the Throne is fifty thousand years, and from the highest heaven of this world to the earth is a thousand years, because the thickness of each heaven is five hundred years, and what is between the lowest part of the heaven and the bottom of the earth is five hundred years. So the meaning is: when the angels ascend from the lowest part of the world to the Throne, the distance of that is fifty thousand years; and if they ascend from this earth in which we are to the inner side of this heaven which is the lowest heaven, the distance of that is a thousand years. What supports this from Ibn ʿAbbas will come at the end of the discussion.

Then Allah, glorified be He, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to be patient, saying: ﴿So be patient with gracious patience﴾. That is: be patient, O Muhammad, over their denial of you and their disbelief in what you have brought, with a gracious patience in which there is no impatience and no complaint to anyone other than Allah. This is the meaning of gracious patience. It was also said: it is that the person afflicted by a calamity is among the people without it being known that he is afflicted. Ibn Zayd and others said: it has been abrogated (naskh, i.e., replaced in ruling) by the verse of the sword.

﴿Indeed, they see it as far off﴾: meaning they see the torment that befalls them as far off, or they see the Day of Resurrection as far off, meaning: not occurring, because they do not believe in it. So the meaning of *baʿidan* (far off) is: deemed remote and impossible. The intended meaning is not that they see it as far but not near.

al-Aʿmash said: they see the resurrection as far off because they do not believe in it, as if they deem it remote by way of impossibility, as you say to one you are debating: "This is far-fetched," meaning: it will not happen.

﴿And We see it as near﴾: meaning We know it to be occurring as near, because what is coming is near.

It was also said: the meaning is: and We see it as easy in Our power, not difficult nor impossible. The sentence is a reason for the command to be patient.

Then Allah, glorified be He, informed when the torment will befall them, saying: ﴿On the day when the sky will be like molten brass﴾. The time expression is connected to an implied element indicated by *waqiʿ* (befalling), or it is a substitute for His saying ﴿on a day﴾, according to the assumption that it is connected to *waqiʿ*; or it is connected to *qarib* (near), or it is determined after it, meaning: on the day when it will be such-and-such. Or it is a substitute for the pronoun in *narahu* (We see it). The first is more likely.

The estimate is: the torment befalls them on the day when the sky will be like *al-muhl*. *Al-muhl* is what is melted of copper, lead, and silver.

Mujahid said: it is pus from the matter and blood.

ʿIkrima and others said: it is the dregs of oil. Its explanation has already been given in Surat al-Kahf and al-Dukhan.

﴿And the mountains will be like wool of various colors﴾: meaning like dyed wool. *ʿIhn* (wool) is not said of wool unless it is dyed.

al-Hasan said: the mountains will be like *ʿihn*, which is red wool, the weakest of wool. It was also said: *ʿihn* is wool of various colors, so He likened the mountains to it in their being of various colors, as in His saying: ﴿white and red streaks of various colors, and jet-black﴾ [Fatir: 27]. When they are carded and scattered into the air, they resemble carded *ʿihn* when the wind scatters it.

﴿And no close friend will ask a close friend﴾: meaning no relative will ask his relative about his condition on that day, because of the terrors that have befallen them, which distract the relative from his relative and the intimate friend from his intimate friend, as He, glorified be He, said: ﴿For every person among them on that day is a matter that occupies him﴾ [ʿAbasa: 37]. It was also said: the meaning is: no close friend asks about a close friend; the preposition was deleted and the verb was connected directly.

The majority read *la yasʾalu* in the active voice. It was said: the second object is omitted, and the estimate is: he does not ask him for his help nor his intercession. Abu Jaʿfar, Abu Haywa, Shayba, and Ibn Kathir in one narration read it in the passive voice. al-Bazzi transmitted this reading from ʿAsim, and the meaning is: no close friend is asked to bring his close friend (into presence). It was also said: this reading is by dropping the preposition, meaning: no close friend is asked about a close friend, rather every person asks about himself and about his deeds.

The clause ﴿they will be made to see them﴾ is either a resumed sentence, or an attribute of *hamim* (close friend), meaning: every close friend is made to see his close friend, and none of them is hidden from another.

There is no creature in the Resurrection but it is before the eyes of its companion. They will not ask one another, nor will any of them speak to another, because each one is occupied with himself. Ibn Zayd said: Allah makes the disbelievers in the Fire see those who misled them in the world, namely the leaders who were followed.

It was also said: His saying "they are made to see them" refers to the angels, meaning: they know the conditions of the people, which are not hidden from them. The pronoun in *yubassaruna-hum* is plural, though the two are the two close friends, in consideration of the general sense, because they are indefinite nouns in a negative context. The majority read *yubassaruna-hum* with the doubled *ba'*, and Qatada read it with the single *ba'*.

Then He, glorified be He, began speech, saying: ﴿The criminal would wish he could ransom himself from the torment of that day with his children﴾. The intended meaning of "criminal" is the disbeliever, or everyone who has committed a sin deserving the Fire. He would wish to ransom himself from the torment of the Day of Resurrection which has befallen him ﴿with his children﴾, ﴿his spouse and his brother﴾, for these are the most beloved people to him and the most honored in his sight. If ransom were accepted from him, he would ransom himself with them and be freed from the torment that has befallen him. The sentence is resumed to explain that the preoccupation of each criminal with himself reaches a point where he wishes to ransom himself from the torment with those mentioned.

The majority read ﴿from the torment of that day﴾ with *ʿadhab* construed as genitive of *yawmi'idhin* (that day). Abu Haywa read *ʿadhabin* with tanwin and cut the genitive construction. The majority read *yawma'idhin* with a kasra on the *mim*, while Nafi', al-Kisa'i, al-Aʿraj, and Abu Haywa read it with a fatha on it.

﴿And his kin who shelters him﴾: meaning his nearest relatives who unite him in lineage or who take him in during hardships, and to whom he takes refuge.

Abu ʿUbayd said: *al-fasila* is less than the *qabila* (tribe).

Tha'lab said: they are his nearest fathers.

al-Mubarrad said: *al-fasila* is a piece of the body's limbs, and a man's clan is called *fasila* by likening it to a part of him.

Malik said: *al-fasila* is the one who raises him.

﴿And whoever is on earth, all of them﴾: meaning the criminal would wish that if he ransomed himself with all who are on earth of the two species (*thaqalan*, i.e., humans and jinn) and others of creation, it would be enough for him.

---

*Note on ʿAdhab and ascending stairways (ma'arij): the Arabic term "ma'arij" is rendered as "ascending stairways," with the Arabic transliteration given in the sense of the plural of "mi'raj" in the commentary's usage.*

Its statement, "Thumma yunjihi" (then it would save him), is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "yaftadi" (would ransom himself): meaning, he would wish to ransom himself, and then the ransom would save him. The conjunction with thumma (then) is used to indicate the improbability of salvation. It has also been said that "yawaddu" (he would wish) requires an answer, as in His statement: ﴿They wish that you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾ [al-Qalam: 9], and the answer here would be "thumma yunjihi." The first view is preferable.

His statement, "Kalla" (No!), is a rebuke to the criminal for that desire, and a clarification that what he wished for, namely the ransom, is impossible. "Kalla" comes with the meaning of "haqqan" (truly), and with the meaning of "la" (no), while including the sense of restraint and rebuke. The pronoun in (p-1530) His statement: ﴿Indeed, it is Laza⦗Laẓā⦘﴾ refers to Jahannam. Its derivation is from talazzi (blazing) in the fire, which is blazing. It has also been said that its origin is lazaẓ, meaning the continuation of punishment, so one of the two ẓā's was changed to an alif. It has also been said that Laẓā is the second rank of the levels of Jahannam.

﴿Nazzā‘atan lilshawā⦘﴾: al-Jumhur read "nazzā‘atun" with a raised vowel (ḍammah), taking it as a second predicate of "inna," or the predicate of an omitted subject, or Laẓā may be a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in the accusative case, and "nazzā‘atun" the predicate of "inna." Or "nazzā‘atun" is an adjective (ṣifah) of Laẓā on the assumption that it is not a proper name. Or the pronoun in "annahā" refers to the event/matter (al-qiṣṣah), so Laẓā is the subject and "nazzā‘atun" its predicate, and the whole sentence is the predicate of "inna." Ḥafṣ on the authority of ‘Āṣim, and Abū ‘Amr in one narration from him, and Abū Ḥaywah, al-Za‘farānī, al-Tirmidhī, and Ibn Miqsam read "nazzā‘atan" with a fatḥah, as a circumstantial (ḥāl).

Abū ‘Alī al-Fārisī said: taking it as a circumstantial is remote, because there is nothing in the sentence that governs the circumstantial. It has been said that the governing element is what the sentence implies of the meaning of blazing, or it is an accusative of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ). Al-Shawā means the extremities, or it is the plural of shawāh, which is the skin of the head, and from it is the verse of al-A‘shā:

"Qālat Qatīlatu mā lahu * qad jullilat shaybān shawātuhu"

Al-Ḥasan and Thābit al-Bunānī said: ﴿nazzā‘atan lilshawā⦘, meaning: it strips away the beauty and comeliness of the face. Abū al-‘Āliyah and Qatādah said likewise: it strips the flesh and skin from the bone, leaving nothing in it.

Al-Kisā’ī said: they are the joints.

Abū Ṣāliḥ said: they are the extremities of the two hands and two feet.

﴿Tad‘ū man adbar⦘, i.e., Laẓā calls whoever turned his back on the truth in the world and ﴿tawallā⦘, i.e., turned away from it.

﴿Wa jama‘a fa-awʿā⦘, i.e., he gathered wealth and put it in a container. It has been said: it will say, "Come to me, O polytheist! Come to me, O hypocrite!" It has also been said: the meaning of "tad‘ū" is "tuhlik" (destroys); the Arabs say, "da‘āka Allāh," i.e., "Allah destroy you." It has also been said: it is not calling by tongue, but its calling them is its capability to punish them. It has also been said: the intended meaning is that the guards of Jahannam call the disbelievers and hypocrites, and the calling is attributed to the Fire, by way of attributing what belongs to the inhabitants to the place. It has also been said: it is a figure of speech and imagery, with no actual calling; the meaning is that their final destination is to it, as the poet said:

"Wa laqad habaṭnā al-wād bayna quwādinā * nad‘ū al-anīsa bihi al-ghaṣīṣu al-abkamu"

Al-Ghaṣīṣ al-abkam is the fly, and it does not call. In this there is a censure of one who gathers wealth, stores it, hoards it, and does not spend it in the paths of good, or does not pay its zakāt.

Al-Firyābī, ‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Nasā’ī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ‘Abbās concerning His statement: ﴿A questioner asked⦘, he said: it is al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, who said, "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky."

And concerning His statement: ﴿with a punishment that will befall⦘, he said: it will occur to the disbelievers, and none can repel it from Allah. ﴿The Lord of the ascending stairways⦘, he said: the Lord of the degrees.

‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him concerning His statement: ﴿A questioner asked⦘, he said: "Sāla" is a valley in Jahannam.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him also concerning His statement: ﴿The Lord of the ascending stairways⦘, he said: the Lord of exaltedness and bounties.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from him also concerning His statement: ﴿in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years⦘, he said: the extent of His command from the lowest of the earths to the extent of His command from above the seven heavens is the measure of fifty thousand years. And ﴿a Day whose measure is a thousand years⦘ [al-Sajdah: 5], he said: it means the command descends from the sky to the earth and ascends from the earth to the sky in one day, and that is the measure of a thousand years, because the distance between the sky and the earth is a journey of five hundred years.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim also reported from him, saying: the thickness of each earth is five hundred years, the thickness of each heaven is five hundred years, the distance between each earth is five hundred years, and from heaven to heaven is five hundred years; that is His statement: ﴿in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years⦘.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th reported from him also concerning His statement: ﴿in a Day whose measure is a thousand years of what you count⦘, he said: this is in the world, where the angels ascend in a day whose measure is a thousand years of what you count. And concerning His statement: ﴿in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years⦘, this is the Day of Resurrection, which Allah made for the disbeliever to be the measure of fifty thousand years.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Bayhaqī reported from him also concerning His statement: ﴿in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years⦘, he said: If you were to measure it, it would be fifty thousand years of your days.

He said: meaning the Day of Resurrection.

We have already mentioned from Ibn ‘Abbās the pause in combining the two verses in Sūrat al-Sajdah.

Aḥmad, Abū Ya‘lā, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th reported from Abū Sa‘īd al-Khudrī, who said: It was said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years⦘, how long this day is!" He said: "By He in whose hand is my soul, it will be made light for the believer until it is easier for him than an obligatory prayer he prays in the world."

In its chain is Darrāj from Abū al-Haytham, and both are weak.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th reported from Abū Hurayrah, raised (marfū‘): "The length of the Day of Resurrection for the believers is only like the time between Ẓuhr and ‘Aṣr."

al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī in Nawādir al-Uṣūl reported from Ibn ‘Abbās concerning His statement: ﴿So be patient with patience beautiful⦘, he said: do not complain to anyone except Me.

Aḥmad, ‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Khaṭīb in al-Muttafiq wa al-Muftariq, and al-Ḍiyā’ in al-Mukhtārah reported from Ibn ‘Abbās concerning His statement: ﴿On the Day the sky will be like molten brass⦘, he said: like the dregs of oil.

Ibn Jarīr reported from him, he said: ﴿They will be made to see them⦘: some of them will recognize others, and they will know one another, then some of them will flee from others.

Ibn Jarīr also reported from him concerning His statement: ﴿Nazzā‘atan lilshawā⦘, he said: it pulls out the top of the head.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 70, verses 1–18 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan.
Al-Qurtubi said: by consensus.
Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "A surah was revealed in Mecca, [beginning with] *Sa'ala* (one asked)."
Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿A questioner asked about a torment about to befall﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) read *sa'ala* with a hamza, while Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir read it without a hamza. Whoever reads it with a hamza takes it from *al-su'al* (asking), and this is the common usage. It may be that it is an implicit meaning of *al-du'a'* (invoking), which is why it takes the *ba'* (with), as you say *da'awtu li-kadha* (I invoked for such-and-such). The meaning is: a caller invoked against himself a torment about to befall. It is also permissible that it retains its original sense, with the *ba'* meaning *ʿan* (about), as in His saying: ﴿ask about Him one who is informed﴾ [al-Furqan: 59]. As for the one who did not read the hamza, it is either a lightening of the hamza by converting it to an *alif*, in which case its meaning is the meaning of the reading of the one who read the hamza, or it is from *al-sayalan* (flowing), and the meaning is: a valley in Hell flowed, called *Sa'il*, as Zayd ibn Thabit said.

This is supported by the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas: *sala sayl* (a flood flowed). It was also said that *sala* means *iltamasa* (sought), and the meaning is: a seeker sought a torment for the disbelievers, so the *ba'* is extra, as in His saying: ﴿grows with oil﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 20]. The first meaning is the apparent one.

al-Akhfash said: it is said, "We went out asking about so-and-so and with so-and-so."
